messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Bomb Disposal Technician
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 57

**Patient Vignette: Mr. A.**

Mr. A. is a 62-year-old married man, a father of three, and a retired bomb disposal technician. He presents for his fifth session, his posture rigid, his hands resting flat on his knees as if bracing for a tremor. He speaks with a measured, deliberate calm, a voice that once gave orders in the most volatile of environments. The story he tells is not of explosions, but of a slow, invisible poison.

The event occurred twenty-three years ago. Mr. A. was the lead technician on a call involving a suspected chemical munition in a disused warehouse. The device was unstable, leaking a pale, oily liquid. His team wore standard blast suits, but the chemical—later identified as a degraded sulfur mustard agent—was not a blast risk. It was a contact and inhalation hazard. He remembers the moment clearly: a faulty seal on his glove, a bead of liquid on his thumb. He wiped it off, thought nothing of it, and completed the procedure. The device was neutralized. The next morning, his thumb was a weeping, blistering wound. Within a week, his lungs felt lined with sandpaper.

The physical scars healed, mostly. He retired on a medical pension, diagnosed with reactive airways dysfunction syndrome and chronic dermatitis. But the real detonation happened later, in the quiet of his home. For years, he could not enter his own garage without checking the floor for puddles. He would wake at 3:00 a.m., his nostrils burning with the phantom smell of bitter almonds and rotten eggs. He began to hoard industrial-grade cleaning supplies, scrubbing his kitchen counters until the finish wore off. His wife, Grace, would find him standing in the shower, fully clothed, letting the hot water run over him, trying to wash away a contamination that was no longer there.

The nightmares are not of bombs. They are of a slow, creeping fog. In the dream, he is standing in a field of white flowers, and the petals are dissolving into a yellow mist. He cannot move. He watches his own hands turn translucent, then vanish. He wakes gasping, his chest tight, convinced he has been poisoned again. He now refuses to eat any food that is not prepared by Grace, and he will not touch a public door handle without a tissue. He carries a small, sealed plastic bag containing a single, pristine latex glove—a talisman of his former competence.

His occupation is not a past tense; it is a lens. He sees the world as a series of potential hazards, each one a device waiting to be disarmed. He has mapped his neighborhood for "safe zones" (cafés with bleach-clean counters) and "hot zones" (the local pharmacy, where the air smells of rubbing alcohol). He cannot sit with his back to a door. He checks his own pulse obsessively, feeling for the "tick" of a chemical timer.

The PCL-5 score of 57 reflects a profound, daily siege. He avoids the news, particularly stories about industrial accidents or chemical spills. He has stopped attending his grandchildren’s birthday parties, terrified that a child’s runny nose or a whiff of cleaning fluid will trigger a panic attack. He tells me, with a hollow laugh, “I used to disarm bombs for a living. Now I can’t even open a bottle of bleach.”

His marriage is strained. Grace understands the science but cannot reach the man. She found the sealed glove in his pocket last week. He told her it was for "emergencies." She cried. He did not.

Mr. A. is a man who once controlled the most dangerous things in the world. Now, he is controlled by a memory of a single drop of liquid on his thumb. He lives in a state of permanent decontamination, waiting for a second explosion that will never come, but which he cannot convince himself has already passed.
